claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa possess a danger-sensing pathway that is a critical fitness determinant during competition against other bacteria.
source: Previously, we showed that Pseudomonas aeruginosa possess a danger-sensing pathway that is a critical fitness determinant during competition against other bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a previously established finding from the authors' prior work.

claim: Genome-wide screens in P. aeruginosa reveal three conserved and widespread interbacterial antagonism resistance clusters (arc1-3).
source: Here, we conducted genome-wide screens in P. aeruginosa that reveal three conserved and widespread interbacterial antagonism resistance clusters (arc1-3).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the transposon library screening data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Arc1-3 are coordinately activated by the Gac/Rsm danger-sensing system.
source: We find that although arc1-3 are coordinately activated by the Gac/Rsm danger-sensing system, they function independently and provide idiosyncratic defense capabilities, distinguishing them from general stress response pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the transposon screening data showing that arc1-3 genes are under Gac/Rsm control (Figure 1) and immunoblotting showing inducible expression through the Gac/Rsm pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Arc1-3 function independently and provide idiosyncratic defense capabilities.
source: We find that although arc1-3 are coordinately activated by the Gac/Rsm danger-sensing system, they function independently and provide idiosyncratic defense capabilities, distinguishing them from general stress response pathways.
evidence: This is supported by data showing additive effects when genes from different arc operons are inactivated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) and differential protection against specific toxins (Figure 2B).

claim: Arc1-3 are distinguished from general stress response pathways.
source: We find that although arc1-3 are coordinately activated by the Gac/Rsm danger-sensing system, they function independently and provide idiosyncratic defense capabilities, distinguishing them from general stress response pathways.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Arc1-3 mutants survive similarly to wild-type under general stress conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Arc3 family proteins provide specific protection against phospholipase toxins by preventing the accumulation of lysophospholipids.
source: Our findings demonstrate that Arc3 family proteins provide specific protection against phospholipase toxins by preventing the accumulation of lysophospholipids in a manner distinct from previously characterized membrane repair systems.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Arc3A is critical for defense against Tle3 (Figure 2C), and that P. aeruginosa lacking Arc3A accumulates lysophospholipids during Tle3 intoxication (Figure 4A-D).

claim: Arc3 prevents lysophospholipid accumulation in a manner distinct from previously characterized membrane repair systems.
source: Our findings demonstrate that Arc3 family proteins provide specific protection against phospholipase toxins by preventing the accumulation of lysophospholipids in a manner distinct from previously characterized membrane repair systems.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Arc3A does not contribute to PE regeneration from LPE (Figure 4G) and functions independently of the Aas reacylation pathway (Figure 4F).

claim: The response of P. aeruginosa to bacterial threats is analogous to eukaryotic innate immunity, wherein threat detection leads to the activation of specialized defense systems.
source: These findings liken the response of P. aeruginosa to bacterial threats to that of eukaryotic innate immunity, wherein threat detection leads to the activation of specialized defense systems.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the coordinated activation of specialized defense pathways (arc1-3) by a danger-sensing system (Gac/Rsm).

claim: Burkholderia thailandensis fiercely antagonizes P. aeruginosa using its antibacterial T6SS.
source: Prior work by our laboratory has shown that Burkholderia thailandensis (B. thai) fiercely antagonizes P. aeruginosa using its antibacterial T6SS (LeRoux et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated as a previously established finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: 34 genes are critical for the survival of P. aeruginosa specifically while undergoing antagonism by B. thai.
source: Duplicate screening of this library revealed 34 genes critical for the survival of P. aeruginosa specifically while undergoing antagonism by B. thai (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B , Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the transposon library screening experiments shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 25 of the 34 genes critical for P. aeruginosa survival during B. thai antagonism belong to the Gac/Rsm regulon.
source: Strikingly, 25 of these belong to the Gac/Rsm regulon and three additional hits included genes directly involved in the Gac/Rsm signaling system (Goodman et al., 2004; Lapouge et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data (Figure 1A) and comparison with known Gac/Rsm-regulated genes from prior studies.

claim: Disruption of genes encoding GacS and GacA elicited the strongest interbacterial defense defect among all genes in the P. aeruginosa genome.
source: Indeed, disruption of genes encoding GacS and GacA, the central sensor kinase and response regulator required for activation of the pathway, respectively, elicited the strongest interbacterial defense defect among all genes in the P. aeruginosa genome (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the transposon screening data in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Inactivating insertions in retS increased interbacterial competitiveness of P. aeruginosa.
source: On the contrary, inactivating insertions in retS, encoding a hybrid sensor kinase that negatively regulates GacS, increased interbacterial competitiveness.
evidence: This is shown in the transposon screening data in Figure 1A.

claim: Five of the six genes within the PA2536-41 cluster are predicted to encode proteins related to phospholipid biosynthesis or metabolism.
source: Five of the six genes within the PA2536-41 cluster are predicted to encode proteins related to phospholipid biosynthesis or metabolism, including four genes encoding products with significant homology to enzymes required for phosphatidylglycerol synthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the gene cluster shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The PA4317-23 genes co-occur across many species within the Xanthomonadaceae and Pseudomonadaceae.
source: The PA4317-23 genes co-occur across many species within the Xanthomonadaceae and Pseudomonadaceae (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PA4317-23 genes include a predicted MoxR-like AAA+-ATPase and a protein with a von Willebrand factor (VWF) domain.
source: While none of the proteins encoded by this gene cluster have been characterized, they include a predicted MoxR-like AAA+-ATPase and a protein with a von Willebrand factor (VWF) domain.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic predictions of protein domains.

claim: PA5113 and PA5114 co-occur widely across bacterial species.
source: Finally, PA5113 and PA5114 also co-occur widely, and several organisms encode single polypeptides that represent a fusion of the two proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Several organisms encode single polypeptides that represent a fusion of PA5113 and PA5114.
source: Finally, PA5113 and PA5114 also co-occur widely, and several organisms encode single polypeptides that represent a fusion of the two proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The fitness deficiency of the triple arc mutant strain approaches that of the ΔgacS strain.
source: Indeed, the fitness deficiency of this triple mutant strain approaches that of the ∆gacS strain, which lacks Gac/Rsm function entirely (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The Gac/Rsm pathway and discrete functional units under its control are critical for P. aeruginosa survival when antagonized by the T6SS of B. thai.
source: Together, these data reveal that the Gac/Rsm pathway and discrete functional units under its control are critical for P. aeruginosa survival when antagonized by the T6SS of B. thai.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transposon screening and competition assay data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Inactivating Arc2 and Arc3 had no impact on B. thai survival when P. aeruginosa was in excess.
source: Under these conditions, inactivating Arc2 and Arc3 had no impact on B. thai survival.
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 2A.

claim: Arc1 inactivation led to a modest increase in B. thai survival relative to its impact on P. aeruginosa defense.
source: Arc1 inactivation led to an increase in B. thai survival; however, this effect was modest relative to its impact on P. aeruginosa defense (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 2A.

claim: Inactivation of the H1-T6SS increased B. thai survival by approximately four orders of magnitude.
source: In contrast, inactivation of the H1-T6SS increased B. thai survival by approximately four orders of magnitude, eclipsing its impact on P. aeruginosa defense by ~100-fold.
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 2A.

claim: The contributions of Arc1-3 to P. aeruginosa competitiveness during antagonism arise predominately from defensive mechanisms.
source: Together, these finding indicate that the contributions of Arc1-3 to P. aeruginosa competitiveness during antagonism arise predominately from defensive mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the competition assay data showing minimal offensive contribution (Figure 2A).

claim: Tle3 inactivation abrogated the antagonism defense defect of P. aeruginosa lacking Arc3 function.
source: Strikingly, we found that Tle3 inactivation abrogated the antagonism defense defect of P. aeruginosa lacking Arc3 function (Figure 2B), whereas its defense defect was maintained in competition experiments against other toxin-inactivated strains of B. thai.
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 2B.

claim: The survival of P. aeruginosa lacking Arc2 function was significantly restored by deletion of colA in B. thai.
source: In contrast, the survival of P. aeruginosa lacking Arc2 function was significantly restored by deletion of colA in B. thai, while none of the single-effector mutations within B. thai impacted the defense defect of P. aeruginosa lacking Arc1 function.
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 2B.

claim: Arc3A is the gene most critical for P. aeruginosa survival during intoxication by Tle3.
source: Remarkably, this experiment defined arc3A as the gene most critical for P. aeruginosa survival during intoxication by Tle3 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the transposon screening data in Figure 2C.

claim: Arc3A is a large protein containing 35 predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Arc3A is a large protein containing 35 predicted transmembrane domains and lacking residues strongly indicative of enzymatic activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the Arc3A protein sequence shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Arc3A lacks residues strongly indicative of enzymatic activity.
source: Arc3A is a large protein containing 35 predicted transmembrane domains and lacking residues strongly indicative of enzymatic activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the Arc3A protein sequence.

claim: Arc3A is expected to span the periplasm with predicted outer-membrane-anchored N-terminal lipidation and a C-terminal inner-membrane transmembrane helix.
source: With predicted outer-membrane-anchored N-terminal lipidation and a C-terminal inner-membrane transmembrane helix, Arc3A is expected to span the periplasm.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic predictions of protein localization and topology.

claim: Apparent orthologs of Arc3A and Arc3B are encoded by neighboring open-reading frames across an exceptionally wide distribution of bacteria.
source: Neither Arc3A nor Arc3B share significant homology with characterized proteins; however, apparent orthologs of each are encoded by neighboring open-reading frames across an exceptionally wide distribution of bacteria (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Arc3A-related proteins are composed of domain of unknown function 2339 (DUF2339).
source: Arc3A-related proteins are composed of domain of unknown function 2339 (DUF2339), possess large, yet varying numbers of transmembrane segments, and are found in bacteria belonging to most Gram-negative and Gram-positive phyla.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of Arc3A homologs.

claim: Arc3A-related proteins are found in bacteria belonging to most Gram-negative and Gram-positive phyla.
source: Arc3A-related proteins are composed of domain of unknown function 2339 (DUF2339), possess large, yet varying numbers of transmembrane segments, and are found in bacteria belonging to most Gram-negative and Gram-positive phyla.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Arc3B-related proteins are restricted to Gram-negative phyla.
source: Consistent with the predicted N-terminal localization of Arc3B to the outer membrane, its related proteins are restricted to Gram-negative phyla.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B and the requirement for an outer membrane.

claim: Arc3A and Arc3B stably associate.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation studies using epitope-tagged variants of Arc3A and Arc3B encoded at their native chromosomal loci provided evidence that the two proteins stably associate (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments with results shown in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: EstA did not impact P. aeruginosa survival during intoxication by Tle3.
source: Although estA encodes an esterase (Wilhelm et al., 1999), which could have relevance for phospholipase defense, estA was not detected in our co-immunoprecipitation analyses, it did not exhibit differential insertion frequency in our screens, and in-frame deletion of estA did not impact P. aeruginosa survival during intoxication by Tle3 (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including co-IP, Tn-seq, and competition assays shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Four Arc3A-related proteins from other species restored Tle3 defense to a statistically significant degree when expressed in P. aeruginosa Δarc3A.
source: Despite high-sequence divergence that would likely preclude specific interactions with Arc3B or other P. aeruginosa factors, four of these proteins restored Tle3 defense to a statistically significant degree and two provided protection equivalent to that of P. aeruginosa arc3A expressed in the same manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: Inactivation of arc3A in Pseudomonas protegens conferred a strong interbacterial antagonism defense defect specific to B. thai Tle3.
source: We also examined one of these proteins in its native context. Inactivation of arc3A in Pseudomonas protegens conferred a strong interbacterial antagonism defense defect specific to B. thai Tle3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: Proteins in the Arc3A family possess the intrinsic capacity to protect bacteria against Tle3-like toxins.
source: In total, these data strongly suggest that proteins in the Arc3A family possess the intrinsic capacity to protect bacteria against Tle3-like toxins, and potentially phospholipase toxins more broadly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the heterologous complementation data (Figure 3C) and native context data (Figure 3D).

claim: P. aeruginosa lacking Arc3A possessed highly elevated levels of lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE) and monolysocardiolipin (MLCL) in a manner dependent on the activity of Tle3 in B. thai.
source: Strikingly, relative to mixtures containing the wild-type organisms, those containing P. aeruginosa ∆arc3A possessed highly elevated levels of lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE) and monolysocardiolipin (MLCL) in a manner dependent on the activity of Tle3 in B. thai (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the mass spectrometry data in Figure 4A.

claim: Lysophosphatidylglycerol, free fatty acid, and corresponding parent phospholipid levels were not measurably altered by Tle3.
source: Lysophosphatidylglycerol, free fatty acid, and corresponding parent phospholipid levels were not measurably altered by Tle3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the mass spectrometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: P. aeruginosa lacking Arc3B accumulates LPE and MLCL during Tle3 intoxication.
source: Radiographic TLC analysis of the phospholipids generated in these strain competition mixtures confirmed that P. aeruginosa lacking Arc3B accumulates LPE and MLCL during Tle3 intoxication (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is shown in the radiographic TLC data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: B. thai strains undergoing Tle3-based self-intoxication accumulated LPE and MLCL.
source: Samples derived from mixtures composed of a B. thai strain with Tle3 and a derivative strain sensitized to Tle3 intoxication through cognate immunity gene inactivation accumulated LPE and MLCL, mirroring our interspecies competition findings (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in the mass spectrometry data in Figure 4E.

claim: In E. coli, lysophospholipids are transported across the inner membrane by the dedicated transporter LplT, after which they are reacylated by Aas.
source: In E. coli, lysophospholipids are transported across the inner membrane by the dedicated transporter LplT, after which they are reacylated by Aas (Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Both LplT and Aas have been shown to play a critical role in defending E. coli cells from phospholipase attack.
source: Both LplT and Aas have been shown to play a critical role in defending E. coli cells from phospholipase attack (Lin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: In P. aeruginosa, LplT and the acylation domain of Aas are found in a single predicted polypeptide, encoded by PA3267 (aas).
source: In P. aeruginosa, LplT and the acylation domain of Aas are found in a single predicted polypeptide, encoded by PA3267 (aas).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the P. aeruginosa genome.

claim: P. aeruginosa strains lacking both aas and arc3A exhibited a Tle3 defense defect substantially greater than that associated with Arc3A inactivation alone.
source: However, we found that P. aeruginosa strains lacking both aas and arc3A exhibited a Tle3 defense defect substantially greater than that associated with Arc3A inactivation alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 4F.

claim: Aas is required for PE regeneration from LPE.
source: Additionally, we found that Aas is required for PE regeneration from LPE, whereas Arc3A neither contributed to this process, nor could we detect changes in LPE stability upon Arc3A inactivation in the absence of antagonism (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in the PE regeneration assay data in Figure 4G.

claim: Arc3A neither contributed to PE regeneration from LPE, nor could changes in LPE stability be detected upon Arc3A inactivation in the absence of antagonism.
source: Additionally, we found that Aas is required for PE regeneration from LPE, whereas Arc3A neither contributed to this process, nor could we detect changes in LPE stability upon Arc3A inactivation in the absence of antagonism (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in the PE regeneration assay data in Figure 4G.

claim: Arc3 encodes a previously undescribed, widespread and independent pathway that prohibits lysophospholipid accumulation by an interbacterial phospholipase toxin.
source: These findings indicate that arc3 encodes a previously undescribed, widespread and independent pathway that prohibits lysophospholipid accumulation by an interbacterial phospholipase toxin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data showing Arc3's role in preventing lysophospholipid accumulation (Figure 4), its widespread distribution (Figure 3B), and its independence from Aas (Figure 4F-G).

claim: Bacteria possess a multitude of coordinately regulated pathways that provide defense against the threats posed by other bacteria.
source: Our work shows that bacteria also possess a multitude of coordinately regulated pathways that provide defense against the threats posed by other bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the discovery of arc1-3 pathways that are coordinately regulated by Gac/Rsm and provide defense against bacterial threats.

claim: Arc3A is the single cellular factor of P. aeruginosa most critical for defense against a PLA toxin.
source: We found that Arc3A is the single cellular factor of P. aeruginosa most critical for defense against a PLA toxin.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data showing arc3A as the most critical gene for Tle3 defense (Figure 2C).

claim: Phospholipase toxins are ancient and among the most prevalent bacterial toxins known.
source: However, it is notable that phospholipase toxins are ancient and among the most prevalent bacterial toxins known.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about bacterial toxins.

claim: Low Arc3A expression was observed in the absence of Gac/Rsm activation.
source: We observed low Arc3A expression in the absence of Gac/Rsm activation, arguing that its role in PARA serves an adaptive purpose.
evidence: This is based on the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The arc clusters are widely conserved among Bacteria.
source: Our bioinformatic analyses show that the arc clusters are widely conserved among Bacteria, yet the Gac/Rsm pathway is restricted to γ-Proteobacteria.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: The Gac/Rsm pathway is restricted to γ-Proteobacteria.
source: Our bioinformatic analyses show that the arc clusters are widely conserved among Bacteria, yet the Gac/Rsm pathway is restricted to γ-Proteobacteria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the distribution of the Gac/Rsm pathway.

claim: The Gac/Rsm pathway post-transcriptionally controls the expression of nearly 400 genes.
source: PARA is coordinated by the Gac/Rsm global regulatory pathway, which post-transcriptionally controls the expression of nearly 400 genes (Goodman et al., 2004; Lapouge et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited references.

claim: The H1-T6SS enables P. aeruginosa to kill or disable competing bacteria through the delivery of a cocktail of toxic effector proteins.
source: This regulon includes the Hcp secretion island I-encoded type VI secretion system (H1-T6SS), the activity of which enables P. aeruginosa to kill or disable competing bacteria through the delivery of a cocktail of toxic effector proteins (Hood et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: P. aeruginosa strains lacking functionality of the two-component system required to initiate Gac/Rsm signaling are severely crippled in interbacterial antagonism defense relative to those lacking only the H1-T6SS.
source: While an important component of PARA, data suggest that the H1-T6SS is just one feature of the response; P. aeruginosa strains lacking functionality of the two-component system required to initiate Gac/Rsm signaling are severely crippled in interbacterial antagonism defense relative to those lacking only the H1-T6SS (LeRoux et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated as a previously established finding from a cited reference.

claim: The majority of the genes under Gac/Rsm control encode proteins of unknown function.
source: The majority of the genes under Gac/Rsm control encode proteins of unknown function, and we hypothesized that these could represent uncharacterized, novel mechanisms by which P. aeruginosa defends against interbacterial antagonism.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study based on prior knowledge of the Gac/Rsm regulon.

claim: A subpopulation of P. aeruginosa cells are lysed during antagonism, releasing intracellular contents that trigger the response in neighboring survivors.
source: The response is activated when a subpopulation of P. aeruginosa cells are lysed, releasing intracellular contents that trigger the response in neighboring survivors (LeRoux et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated as a previously established finding from a cited reference.

claim: Orphan immunity proteins share homology with and are likely evolved from cognate immunity proteins that protect bacteria from undergoing self-intoxication.
source: These 'orphan' immunity proteins share homology with and are likely evolved from cognate immunity proteins that protect bacteria from undergoing self-intoxication, which is inherent to the indiscriminate nature of the T6SS delivery mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about orphan immunity proteins.

claim: Extracellular polysaccharide capsules protect Vibrio cholerae and Escherichia coli from T6SS-based attack of other species.
source: Extracellular polysaccharide capsules protect Vibrio cholerae and Escherichia coli from T6SS-based attack of other species (Hersch et al., 2020b; Toska et al., 2018), and in Acinetobacter baumannii, lysine modification at peptidoglycan crosslinks was suggested to render the cell wall resistant to degradation by amidase toxins (Le et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited references.

claim: In Acinetobacter baumannii, lysine modification at peptidoglycan crosslinks was suggested to render the cell wall resistant to degradation by amidase toxins.
source: Extracellular polysaccharide capsules protect Vibrio cholerae and Escherichia coli from T6SS-based attack of other species (Hersch et al., 2020b; Toska et al., 2018), and in Acinetobacter baumannii, lysine modification at peptidoglycan crosslinks was suggested to render the cell wall resistant to degradation by amidase toxins (Le et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Bacterial stress responses evolved in part as a means of detecting and responding to antagonistic competitors.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that bacterial stress responses evolved in part as a means of detecting and responding to antagonistic competitors (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; Lories et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from cited references.

claim: Stress response genes involved in envelope integrity and acid stress can contribute to resistance against a V. cholerae phospholipase toxin in E. coli and P. aeruginosa.
source: A candidate-based approach applied to E. coli and P. aeruginosa found that stress response genes involved in envelope integrity and acid stress, among others, can contribute to resistance against a V. cholerae phospholipase toxin (Kamal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: P. aeruginosa genes that impacted survival when the V. cholerae toxin was produced heterologously did not influence the fitness of the bacterium during interbacterial competition with V. cholerae.
source: While the P. aeruginosa genes identified impacted survival when the toxin was produced heterologously within the organism, they did not influence the fitness of the bacterium during interbacterial competition with V. cholerae.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference (Kamal et al., 2020).

claim: B. thai delivers a cocktail of toxins to target cells including two predicted phospholipases (Tle1 and Tle3), a peptidoglycan-degrading amidase (Tae2) and a colicin-like toxin predicted to form inner membrane pores (ColA).
source: Notably, B. thai delivers a cocktail of toxins to target cells including two predicted phospholipases (Tle1 and Tle3) (Russell et al., 2013), a peptidoglycan-degrading amidase (Tae2) and a colicin-like toxin predicted to form inner membrane pores (ColA) (Russell et al., 2012; Salomon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited references.

claim: Enzymes with PLA activity cleave glycerophospholipids at the sn1 or sn2 position, generating fatty acid and detergent-like lysophospholipid products.
source: Enzymes with PLA activity cleave glycerophospholipids at the sn1 or sn2 position, generating fatty acid and detergent-like lysophospholipid products (Filkin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: For toxins like Tle3, which are delivered to target cells in exceedingly low quantities, it is likely toxic products, rather than phospholipid depletion per se, that most immediately contribute to cell death.
source: For toxins like Tle3, which are delivered to target cells in exceedingly low quantities (Fridman et al., 2020; Hernandez et al., 2020), it is likely toxic products, rather than phospholipid depletion per se, that most immediately contribute to cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited references about T6SS toxin delivery quantities.

claim: Aas genes neighbor arc3 genes in many bacteria.
source: Interestingly, the aas gene was illuminated as a potential P. aeruginosa antagonism defense factor in two of the transposon mutant screens we performed and aas genes neighbor arc3 genes in many bacteria (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aas overexpression complements the Δaas-dependent defect in the Δarc3A Δaas strain, but it does not compensate for the inactivation of Arc3A.
source: Aas overexpression complements the Δaas-dependent defect in this strain, but it does not compensate for the inactivation of Arc3A (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The number and density of transmembrane helices in Arc3A family proteins is unusual.
source: The number and density of transmembrane helices in Arc3A family proteins is unusual, and we postulate that these anomalous features of the protein are intimately connected to its mechanism of action.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of Arc3A protein structure (Figure 3A).

claim: The transmembrane segments of Arc3A may sequester lysophospholipids and facilitate their turnover.
source: These segments may sequester lysophospholipids and facilitate their turnover or it is conceivable that they directly recruit and interfere with phospholipase enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about Arc3A's mechanism of action.

claim: The transmembrane segments of Arc3A may directly recruit and interfere with phospholipase enzymes.
source: These segments may sequester lysophospholipids and facilitate their turnover or it is conceivable that they directly recruit and interfere with phospholipase enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about Arc3A's mechanism of action.

claim: The survival of strains lacking Arc1-3 function was equivalent to wild-type P. aeruginosa in general stress assays.
source: Unlike previously established stress-intolerant control strains (∆rpoS and ∆vacJ), the survival of strains lacking Arc1-3 function was equivalent to wild-type P. aeruginosa in these assays, suggesting that their function is distinct from those involved in general stress resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the stress assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Basal expression of Arc1-3 is exceedingly low, yet highly inducible through stimulation of the antagonism-responsive Gac/Rsm pathway.
source: This is also in line with the regulatory profile of Arc1-3; immunoblotting showed that basal expression of each is exceedingly low, yet highly inducible through stimulation of the antagonism-responsive Gac/Rsm pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblotting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Arc2 and Arc3 are major defense factors against insults caused by ColA and Tle3, respectively.
source: We found that Arc2 and Arc3 are major defense factors against insults caused by ColA and Tle3, respectively, suggesting that these toxins may damage cells by a mechanism not efficiently countered by other cellular pathways.
evidence: This is based on the competition assay data showing specific defense against these toxins (Figure 2B).

claim: Tle3 and ColA may damage cells by a mechanism not efficiently countered by other cellular pathways.
source: We found that Arc2 and Arc3 are major defense factors against insults caused by ColA and Tle3, respectively, suggesting that these toxins may damage cells by a mechanism not efficiently countered by other cellular pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Arc2 and Arc3 are major defense factors against these specific toxins.

claim: Arc3 provides specific defense against Tle3.
source: These results support the model that Arc3 provides specific defense against Tle3, Arc2 provides a degree of specific protection against ColA, and Arc1 serves a broader role in antagonism defense.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data showing arc3 genes are critical for Tle3 defense but not ColA defense (Figure 2C, D).

claim: Arc2 provides a degree of specific protection against ColA.
source: These results support the model that Arc3 provides specific defense against Tle3, Arc2 provides a degree of specific protection against ColA, and Arc1 serves a broader role in antagonism defense.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data showing arc2 genes contribute to ColA defense (Figure 2D).

claim: Arc1 serves a broader role in antagonism defense.
source: These results support the model that Arc3 provides specific defense against Tle3, Arc2 provides a degree of specific protection against ColA, and Arc1 serves a broader role in antagonism defense.
evidence: This is based on the observation that Arc1 contributes to defense but not in a toxin-specific manner (Figure 2B-D).

claim: Insertions in arc3B crippled P. aeruginosa defense against Tle3, though to a lesser degree than arc3A.
source: Insertions in the second Arc3 gene, arc3B, also crippled P. aeruginosa defense against Tle3, though to a lesser degree.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data in Figure 2C.

claim: Only one gene within Arc1 contributed to Tle3 defense beyond the threefold insertion frequency ratio cutoff.
source: Arc2 genes were dispensable for Tle3 defense, and only one gene within Arc1 contributed to Tle3 defense beyond the threefold insertion frequency ratio cutoff we employed.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data in Figure 2C.

claim: Four of the six Arc2 genes hit in the initial screen provided defense against ColA that exceeded the threefold cutoff.
source: However, four of the six Arc2 genes hit in our initial screen provided defense against ColA that exceeded our threefold cutoff.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data in Figure 2D.

claim: Arc3 genes were wholly dispensable for defense against ColA.
source: Additionally, one Arc1 gene met these criteria, whereas Arc3 genes were wholly dispensable for defense against ColA.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data in Figure 2D.

claim: There is evidence that transcripts containing arc3A, arc3B, and estA are generated by P. aeruginosa.
source: The arc3A and arc3B genes abut a third gene encoded in the same orientation, estA, and there is evidence that transcripts containing all three genes are generated by P. aeruginosa (Gebhardt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: EstA was not detected in co-immunoprecipitation analyses with Arc3A and Arc3B.
source: Although estA encodes an esterase (Wilhelm et al., 1999), which could have relevance for phospholipase defense, estA was not detected in our co-immunoprecipitation analyses, it did not exhibit differential insertion frequency in our screens, and in-frame deletion of estA did not impact P. aeruginosa survival during intoxication by Tle3 (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: EstA did not exhibit differential insertion frequency in the transposon screens.
source: Although estA encodes an esterase (Wilhelm et al., 1999), which could have relevance for phospholipase defense, estA was not detected in our co-immunoprecipitation analyses, it did not exhibit differential insertion frequency in our screens, and in-frame deletion of estA did not impact P. aeruginosa survival during intoxication by Tle3 (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data in Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 1 and 2.

claim: Arc3A proteins are found in bacteria lacking an Arc3B homolog.
source: The observation that Arc3A proteins are found in bacteria lacking an Arc3B homolog, combined with our finding that Arc3B contributes relatively little to Tle3 defense, led us to speculate that Arc3A plays an intrinsic role in defense, independent of its interaction Arc3B.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Arc3B contributes relatively little to Tle3 defense.
source: The observation that Arc3A proteins are found in bacteria lacking an Arc3B homolog, combined with our finding that Arc3B contributes relatively little to Tle3 defense, led us to speculate that Arc3A plays an intrinsic role in defense, independent of its interaction Arc3B.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data (Figure 2C) and competition assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Two Arc3A-related proteins from other species provided protection equivalent to that of P. aeruginosa arc3A when expressed in P. aeruginosa Δarc3A.
source: Despite high-sequence divergence that would likely preclude specific interactions with Arc3B or other P. aeruginosa factors, four of these proteins restored Tle3 defense to a statistically significant degree and two provided protection equivalent to that of P. aeruginosa arc3A expressed in the same manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: Arc3B may play an auxiliary role in defense that is only detectable under the more stringent conditions of the Tn-seq screens.
source: These results suggest that Arc3B may play an auxiliary role in defense that is only detectable under the more stringent conditions of the Tn-seq screens, where P. aeruginosa strains compete with each other as well as B. thai.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between Tn-seq results (showing arc3B contribution) and pairwise competition results (not showing arc3B contribution).

claim: In two Tn-seq screens, a significant difference in arc3B insertion frequency was observed during competition with wild-type B. thai compared to the T6SS- or Tle3-inactivated mutants.
source: In two of our Tn-seq screens (Figure 1A and C, Figure 2C), we observed a significant difference in arc3B insertion frequency during competition with wild-type B. thai compared to the T6SS- or Tle3-inactivated mutants.
evidence: This is based on the transposon screening data in Figure 1A, C and Figure 2C.

claim: In pairwise competition experiments with B. thai, no significant fitness defect was detected associated with arc3B inactivation in either the wild-type or the Δarc3A background.
source: However, in pairwise competition experiments with B. thai, we were unable to detect a significant fitness defect associated with arc3B inactivation in either the wild-type or the Δarc3A background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the competition assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
